title: Every Order ID, Once
description:
`source_orders` is the live production system; `warehouse_orders` is what landed in the analytics warehouse after the last sync. They're supposed to agree, but don't always.

Report every distinct `order_id` that appears in **either** system, with no duplicates even if an id appears in both.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: `source_orders` has ids 1, 2, 3, 4. `warehouse_orders` has ids 1, 2, 5. Put them together and drop duplicates: 1 and 2 appear in both but only count once each, 3 and 4 only came from source, and 5 only came from the warehouse. That gives the 5-row result: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. If you used `UNION ALL` instead, 1 and 2 would each show up twice — this problem specifically wants each id listed once, which is what plain `UNION` does automatically.
hint: Plain UNION already removes duplicates across the two SELECTs — you don't need DISTINCT on top of it.

title: Present In Both Systems
description:
Report every `order_id` that appears in **both** `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders`.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: `source_orders` has ids 1, 2, 3, 4; `warehouse_orders` has ids 1, 2, 5. The only ids sitting in *both* lists are 1 and 2 — order 3 and 4 never made it to the warehouse, and order 5 in the warehouse doesn't exist in source at all (maybe it was entered directly there by mistake). So the result is just [1, 2]: the ids every system agrees actually exist.
hint: INTERSECT keeps only rows present in both SELECTs — exactly "in both systems".

title: Orders That Never Synced
description:
Report every `order_id` that exists in `source_orders` but is **missing** from `warehouse_orders` — orders that failed to sync.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Start from every id in `source_orders` — 1, 2, 3, 4 — and cross off any that also show up in `warehouse_orders` (1 and 2 both do). What's left is 3 and 4: orders that exist in the live system but were never synced to the warehouse. Order 5 doesn't appear here at all — it's a warehouse-only id, and EXCEPT only ever removes from the *first* list, it never adds anything from the second.
hint: EXCEPT is one-directional: `A EXCEPT B` means "in A, remove anything also in B". Order of the two SELECTs matters here.

title: Out Of Sync, Either Direction
description:
Report every `order_id` that is out of sync between `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders` **in either direction** — present in one system but not the other.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: This combines the previous two ideas. Source-only ids (source EXCEPT warehouse) are 3 and 4. Warehouse-only ids (warehouse EXCEPT source) are just 5. Union those two lists together and you get [3, 4, 5] — every id that's out of sync in *some* direction, whichever way. Order 1 and 2 are missing from this result on purpose: they're in both systems, so they're not "out of sync" at all.
hint: This is a symmetric difference: one EXCEPT for each direction, combined with UNION. Careful — chained set operators evaluate left-to-right at equal precedence in SQLite, not "EXCEPT before UNION". `A EXCEPT B UNION C EXCEPT D` means `((A EXCEPT B) UNION C) EXCEPT D`, not two independent EXCEPTs joined by UNION. SQLite won't let you parenthesize compound-select operands directly either — wrap each EXCEPT as its own subquery in FROM instead.

title: Count Out-Of-Sync Orders By Direction
description:
Report how many orders are out of sync **in each direction** between `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders`: how many exist only in source, and how many exist only in the warehouse.

Name the columns `direction` (`source_only` or `warehouse_only`) and `n`. Return exactly two rows, in any order.
outputExplanation: Same two groups as the previous problem — source-only is {3, 4}, a count of 2; warehouse-only is {5}, a count of 1 — but instead of listing the actual ids, this one summarizes each direction as one labeled row: `('source_only', 2)` and `('warehouse_only', 1)`. Two rows, always, even here where the counts happen to differ — and even if they'd been equal, UNION ALL guarantees you'd still get two separate rows instead of one row silently swallowing the other.
hint: Use UNION ALL here, not UNION — you want exactly one row per direction even if both counts happen to be equal (UNION would collapse them into one row).

title: Orders That Fully Agree
description:
An order only "fully agrees" between systems if **both** its `order_id` and its `amount` match. Report every `(order_id, amount)` pair that appears in both `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders` exactly as-is.

Name the columns `order_id` and `amount`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Order 1 is $120 in both `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders` — a genuine match, both columns agree. Order 2 is $80 in both — also a match. Orders 3 and 4 don't even exist in the warehouse, so they can't match anything there. The result is exactly those two full-agreement pairs: (1, 120) and (2, 80). If order 1 had been recorded as $125 in the warehouse instead, INTERSECT would drop it entirely — matching order_id alone isn't enough, both columns in the pair have to agree.
hint: INTERSECT compares whole rows (every selected column together), not just the first one — an order_id match with a different amount will not survive here.

title: Build An Audit Log Of Both Systems
description:
Build a combined audit log listing every row from `source_orders` and every row from `warehouse_orders`, tagged with which system it came from. Unlike the reconciliation queries above, **duplicate rows must be preserved** here — if source has the same order twice, the log should show it twice.

Name the columns `order_id`, `customer_name`, `amount` and `system` (`source` or `warehouse`). Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: `source_orders` has 4 rows, `warehouse_orders` has 3 rows — the audit log is simply all 7 of them, each tagged with where it came from: the 4 source rows tagged `'source'`, then the 3 warehouse rows tagged `'warehouse'`. Notice order 1 and order 2 each appear *twice* in this output — once per system — even though they represent the "same" order. That's intentional here: an audit log is a record of what each system reported, not a deduplicated reconciliation view like the earlier problems.
hint: This is exactly the case UNION ALL exists for — an audit log should never silently drop a real duplicate row the way UNION would.

title: Three-Way Reconciliation
description:
There are now **three** systems: `source_orders`, `warehouse_orders` and `vendor_orders`. For every `order_id` that appears in at least one of them, report how many of the three systems contain it.

Name the columns `order_id` and `system_count`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS system_count
FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM source_orders
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM warehouse_orders
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM vendor_orders
)
GROUP BY order_id;
outputExplanation:
Looking at the example data, walk through each `order_id` and count how many of the three tables it shows up in:

- **1** — in `source_orders`, `warehouse_orders`, *and* `vendor_orders` → all three systems have it → `system_count = 3`.
- **2** — in `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders`, but not `vendor_orders` → two systems → `system_count = 2`.
- **3** — in `source_orders` and `vendor_orders`, but not `warehouse_orders` → two systems → `system_count = 2`.
- **4** — only in `source_orders` → one system → `system_count = 1`.
- **5** — only in `warehouse_orders` → one system → `system_count = 1`.
- **6** — only in `vendor_orders` → one system → `system_count = 1`.

Notice order `4` never appears in `warehouse_orders` or `vendor_orders` at all, yet it still shows up in the output with `system_count = 1` — the question asks for every order_id that appears in **at least one** system, not just the ones every system agrees on.
hint: DISTINCT the order_ids from each system *before* combining them with UNION ALL — otherwise a duplicate row inside one system's own table would inflate its count, when it should only ever count as "present" once per system.

title: Match Customers Despite Messy Formatting
description:
The same customer is recorded with inconsistent formatting across systems — `'Ann Lee'` in one, `'ANN LEE'` or `'  ann lee '` in another. Report every customer name (normalized to lowercase with no leading/trailing whitespace) that appears in **both** `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders`, once formatting differences are accounted for.

Name the column `customer`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: In this particular example, the names already happen to be spelled identically in both tables — 'Ann Lee' and 'Ben Kim' appear the same way in `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders` — so after lowercasing and trimming, INTERSECT finds 'ann lee' and 'ben kim' in both. The point of the LOWER/TRIM normalization doesn't really show up until messier data: a hidden test case has names like `'  ben kim '` in one table and `'BEN KIM'` in another — without normalizing first, a plain INTERSECT on the raw text would miss that match entirely, since 'Ben Kim' and '  ben kim ' are different strings byte-for-byte.
hint: Normalize both sides the same way (LOWER + TRIM) before comparing — INTERSECT on the raw customer_name column would miss matches that are really the same person.

title: Reconcile Despite Duplicate-Row Noise
description:
A sync bug sometimes inserts the same order into `source_orders` twice. That duplication is not a real discrepancy and must not be reported as one. Report every `order_id` that is genuinely out of sync between `source_orders` and `vendor_orders` — present in one but not the other — regardless of how many times a row happens to be duplicated on either side.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: This time it's `source_orders` (ids 1, 2, 3, 4) versus `vendor_orders` (ids 1, 3, 6) — a different pair of systems than the earlier problems. Source-only ids are 2 and 4 (vendor never mentions them); vendor-only is just 6 (source never mentions it). Union those together and the result is [2, 4, 6]. Order 1 and 3 are in both, so they're correctly excluded — and a hidden test case duplicates order 1's row inside `source_orders` on purpose, to confirm that an accidental double-insert doesn't trick this query into reporting a false discrepancy.
hint: A row-count comparison ("source has 5 rows, vendor has 4") would be fooled by the duplicate. EXCEPT and UNION both operate on distinct sets, so a plain symmetric difference is naturally immune to duplicate noise — no extra DISTINCT needed. Just wrap each EXCEPT as its own subquery in FROM, since chained set operators are otherwise evaluated left-to-right rather than nesting the way you'd expect.
